la:verb:dirigo.gloss: to lay straight; arrange in lines (especially in military contexts)
senses: to lay straight; arrange in lines (especially in military contexts)
to direct to a place, guide, steer
la:verb:dirigo.html:
dī-rĭgo or dērĭgo (the latter form preferred by Roby, L. G. 2, p. 387; cf. Rib. Proleg. ad Verg. p. 401 sq.; so ; ; Weissenb.; Drak.; Lach. ad ; Ritter; acc. to Brambach, s. v., the two forms are different words, de-rigo meaning
to give a particular direction to; di-rigo, to arrangein distinct lines, set or move different ways; cf. describo and discribo. But the distinction is not observed in the MSS. and edd. generally), rexi, rectum, 3 (perf. sync. direxti, ), v. a.
dis-rego
, to lay straight, set in a straight line, to arrange, draw up (class.; cf.: guberno, collineo, teneo).
Lit.
In gen.: coronam si diviseris, arcus erit: si direxeris, virga,: haec directa materia injecta consternebantur,: crates,: naves ante portum,; cf.: naves in pugnam,: vicos,i. e. to build regularly,; cf. castella,: molem recta fronte, et saep.: regiones lituo,i. e. to lay out, bound,; cf.: finem alicui veterem viam regiam,.—Esp. freq.: aciem,to draw up the troops in battle array,; ; ; ; et saep.; cf. frontem,; : membrana plumbo derecta,ruled with a lead-pencil,.—*
Perh. i. q., to split, cleave in twain: elephantum machaeră dirigit, (dub.); cf.: dirigere apud Plautum invenitur pro discidere, Paul. ex Müll.—
In partic., with respect to the terminus, to send in a straight line, to direct to a place (so most freq.): ex vestigio vela ad castra Corneliana,: aciem ad te,: cursum ad litora,: iter ad Mutinam, Planc. ap. et saep.—Afterwards more freq. with in: equum in consulem,: currum in hostem,: tela manusque in corpus Aeacidae,; : hastam in te,; cf.: dentes in inguina,: cursum in Africam,: cursum per auras in lucos, et saep.: navem eo,: gressum huc,; et saep.; and poet. with the dat.: Ilo hastam, et saep.—Without designating the limit: ab iisdem (Etesiis) maritimi cursus (i. e. navium) celeres et certi diriguntur,to be directed, steered,: iter navis,: cursum,; esp. freq. of weapons, to aim, direct: spicula,; : hastile,: tela,: sagittas, et saep.—Poet.: vulnera,; Drak.; ; cf.: vulnera alicui,.
Trop.
In gen., to set in order, arrange (very rare): materias divisione dirigere,.—Far more freq. (esp. in Cic. and Quint.),
In partic.: aliquid ad or in aliquid; also: aliqua re, to direct, guide, arrange a thing either to something (as its aim, scope) or according to something (as its rule or pattern).
With ad: meas cogitationes sic dirigo, non ad illam parvulam Cynosuram sed, etc., Ac. 2, 20, 66; cf.: orationem ad exempla,; : judicium ad ea,: se ad id quod, etc.,; cf.: se ad ea effingenda,: praecipua rerum ad famam, et saep.—In a different sense (viz., with ad equiv. to secundum, v. ad): in verbis et eligendis et collocandis nihil non ad rationem,: vitam ad certam rationis normam,to conform,: leges hominum ad naturam,; et saep.—
With in (not so in Cic.): tota mente (intentionem) in opus ipsum,: communes locos in vitia,; et saep.—
With abl. (only in Cic.): quos (fines) utilitate aut voluptate dirigunt,: omnia voluptate,: utilitatem honestate,: haec normā,.—
Without an object: (divinatio) ad veritatem saepissime dirigit, —(ε) With acc. only: epistolam (sc. ad aliquem), to write, Capit. Clod. Alb. 2.—(ζ) With adversus, .—Hence, dīrectus (dērectus), a, um, P. a., made straight, straight, direct, whether horizontally or perpendicularly; straight, level; upright, steep.
Lit.: auditus flexuosum iter habet, ne quid intrare possit, si simplex et directum pateret,; cf. aes (tubae), opp. flexum,: iter,: latera, ; cf. trabes,: ordo (olearum),: arcus (opp. obliquus),: paries,i. e. that cuts another at right angles,: ut directiores ictus flant, Quadrig. ap. : praeruptus locus utraque ex parte directus,; cf. : (Henna) ab omni aditu circumcisa atque directa, Zumpt N. cr.: cornu,.—Subst.: dī-rectum, i, n., a straight line: in directo pedum VIII. esse, in anfracto XVI.,in a straight line, Müll.; so, altitudo (montis) per directum IV. M. pass.,; cf. : cadere in directum moderate (with exire per devexum),; —
Trop., straightforward, unceremonious, open, simple, direct: o praeclaram beate vivendi et apertam et simplicem et directam viam,; cf.: iter ad laudem,: vera illa et directa ratio,: tristis ac directus senex,; cf.: quid est in judicio? Directum, asperum, simplex, SI PARET HS ICCC DARI,: percunctatio et denuntiatio belli,; cf. contiones, (v. obliquus): verba,: actio,; et saep.; cf. institutio (opp. precaria),: libertates (opp. fideicommissariae),.—Adv.
dīrectē, directly, straight (very rare): dicere,: ire,.—Far more freq.,
dīrectō, directly, straight: deorsum ferri,: transversas trabes,: ad fidem spectare,; so (opp. anfractus and circuitio); ; ; —*
dīrectā: quo magis ursimus alte directā,press deep down perpendicularly,.—
dīrectim, straightway, directly (post-class.), ; fin.—Comp.: directius gubernare,.—Sup. seems not to occur either in the adj. or in the adv.

la:verb:dirumpo.gloss: to break down, to wear away
senses: to break down, to wear away
la:verb:dirumpo.html:
dī-rumpo or disr-, rūpi, ruptum, 3,
v. a., to break or dash to pieces; to break, burst asunder (rare but class.).
Lit.: tabulā caput,: ne medius disrumpar miser,: cum se in nubem induerint (venti) ejusque tenuissimam quamque partem coeperint dividere atque disrumpere,: imagines,: homo diruptus, i. e. that has a rupture (c. c. dirutus), .—In an obscene sense, —
Trop.
To break off, sunder, sever: amicitias exorsa aliqua offensione dirumpimus,; cf.: humani generis societatem,: regnum,.—And in a figure borrowed from a play (in which two persons tugged at the ends of a rope until it broke, or one of them fell to the ground): cave dirumpatis, i. e. the rope or thread of your recollection,.— Esp. freq.,
Pass. in colloquial lang., to burst with envy, etc.: unum omnia posse dirumpuntur ii qui, etc.,; cf.: infinito fratris tui plausu dirumpitur,: dirumpor dolore,; cf. risu,.—Once act.: dirupi me paene, I nearly burst myself with earnest speaking, .

la:adj:dirus.html:
dīrus, a, um, adj.
Sanscr. root dī, to flee; Gr. δέος, δείδω, δεινός
,
fearful, awful (for syn. cf.: saevus, atrox, ferox, crudelis, trux, furens, furiosus, immitis).
Orig. belonging to the lang. of augurs; of fate, ill-omened, ominous, boding, portentous: QVAE AVGVR INIVSTA, NEFASTA VITIOSA DIRA DEFIXERIT, IRRITA INFECTAQVE SVNTO,; cf. : tristissima exta sine capite fuerunt, quibus nihil videtur esse dirius,fin.; cf.: bubo, dirum mortalibus omen,: omen,; ; : aves,; : alites,: somnia,: tempus, Cic. Poët. Div. 1, 11, 18: exsecrationes,; ; ; cf. deprecationes,: detestatio,: ritus sacrorum,: religio loci, et saep.—Hence, as subst.:
dīrae, ārum, f.
(sc. res), ill-boding things, portents, unlucky signs: dirarum obnuntiatio,; ; ; ; ; Müll. Etrusk. 2, p. 117.—
As a nom. propr., Dīrae, the Furies, ; ; ; ; called also Dirae deae, sorores, and 454.—
dīra, ōrum, n., fearful things, ill-boding events: in dira et in vitiosa incurrimus,; ; cf.: me mihi dira precari cogis,to curse, invoke curses on,: dira passus,.
Transf., of character, dreadful, horrible, terrible, abominable, detestable (so almost exclusively poet.; a very favorite expression with the Aug. poets; in the Ciceron. per. not at all; but cf. diritas, II.): senex dirissimus, Varr. Poët. ap. : Dea,i. e. Circe,: Ulixes,; : Hannibal,: durum, (also ap. ): Afer,: Amulius,: noverca,: pellex, et saep.: hydra,: serpens,: victima,: parens,fell, cruel,: soror,: parentes,.—
Of inanimate and abstr. subjects: regio,: facies,: dapes,: venena,; : Asphaltites lacus,: scopulus,: duarum Syrtium vadoso mari diri sinus, et saep.: bellum,: nefas,: sollicitudines,: amores,: superbia,: quies, et saep.—Poet., answering to the Gr. δεινός, with inf.: dira portas quassare trabs,.—
Skilful: in complicandis negotiis,.

la:verb:diripio.gloss: to tear apart; to tear to pieces
senses: to tear apart; to tear to pieces
to lay waste, plunder an enemy’s territory or possessions
to run after; to compete for the company of
la:verb:diripio.html:
dī-rĭpĭo, ŭi, eptum, 3, v. a.
rapio
,
to tear asunder, tear in pieces (class.).
In gen. (rarely): Pentheum diripuisse aiunt Bacchas,: Hippolytum (equi),; : nec opinantes (leae),: membra manibus nefandis, et saep.: venti diripiunt fretum,. —
In partic.
Milit. t. t., to lay waste, ravage, spoil, plunder an enemy's territory or possessions (so most freq.): bona alicujus,; ; : magnum numerum frumenti commeatusque,: impedimenta,: naves more praedonum,: praedas bellicas, et saep.: oppidum,; fin.: urbes,: tecta,: templa hostiliter,; cf.: castra hostiliter,; and: oppida hostiliter,: civitates,: provincias,: patriam, et saep.—
With personal objects: Eburones,; : Lusitanos,: ab hostibus diripi,; cf. —
Transf. beyond the milit. sphere, to destroy, to rob: (Harpyiae) diripiunt dapes,: supellectilem,.—
To struggle, strive, contend for a thing (post-Aug.): talos jecit in medium, quos pueri diripere coeperant,: editum librum, to buy up rapidly, Suet. Vita Pers. fin.—Of persons: diripitur ille toto foro patronus,; so, Timagenem, id. de Ira, 3, 23: Homerum (urbes),: matrem avidis complexibus ambo,: te potentiores per convivia,.—
To tear away, snatch away: direpto ex capite regni insigni et lacerata veste,: ferrum a latere,; Stallb. (al. derepta). —
Trop., of the mind and feelings, to distract, distress: differor, distrahor, diripior,.

la:verb:dirimo.html:
dĭrĭmo, ēmi, emptum (
perf. dirempsi, cited as error, P.), 3, v. a.
disĕmo, like diribeo, from dis-habeo
, to take apart; to part, separate, divide (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense—cf.: findo, scindo, divello, separo, sejungo, segrego, secerno).
Lit.: dirimi corpus distrahive,; cf. : Tiberis Veientem agrum a Crustumino dirimens,; cf.: castris Ilerdam,: sontes justis (Minos), Claud. ap. : oppida nostra unius diei itinere dirimuntur,are separated from each other,; cf.: urbs Vulturno flumine dirempta,; and: dirempta mari gens,; and absol.: dirimente amne, et saep.—Poet., of cutting through the waves in a ship, .
Trop.
To break off, interrupt, to disturb, put off, delay (the fig. is taken from combatants who are parted asunder; transferred, like the opp. committere, to things; cf.: dirimere infestas acies, dirimere iras,): proelium tandem diremit nox,; so, proelium,; ; ; ; cf. : pugnam,: bellum,; ; : certamina, et saep.: controversiam,i. e. to adjust, compose,: seditionem,: litem,: rem arbitrio, et saep.; also, to separate, dissolve, break off a connection: conjunctionem civium,: societatem,; : nuptias,: affinitatem,: amicitias,; cf. : caritatem quae est inter natos et parentes,: pacem,; : conubium, et saep.—So too, to interrupt, disturb, break up a conversation, deliberation, etc.: colloquium,: sermonem,: concilia populi,: comitia,; cf. absol.: actum est eo die nihil: nox diremit,.—
In gen., to destroy, frustrate, bring to naught: natura animaï morte dirempta,: auspicium,; cf.: rem susceptam,: dirimere

tempus et proferre diem, : ea res consilium diremit,fin.— Absnl., to dissuade, to be unfavorable: dirimen tibus auspicibus,.

la:adj:directus.gloss: laid straight, arranged in lines, having been arranged in lines
senses: laid straight, arranged in lines, having been arranged in lines

la:verb:diruo.gloss: to overthrow, demolish, destroy, ruin down
senses: to overthrow, demolish, destroy, ruin down
la:verb:diruo.html:
dī-rŭo, rŭi, rŭtum, 3,
v. a., to tear asunder, overthrow, demolish, destroy (class. —cf.: deleo, diluo, exstinguo, everto, demolior).
Prop.: maceriam,: urbem,; ; ; et saep.: muros,: templa,: arcum circi,: monumentum,; : fores ira, . arbusta,: regna Priami, (3, 26, 8 M.); cf. (5), 1, 113 et saep.— Absol.: diruit, aedificat,; cf.: nova diruunt, alia aedificant,.—Hyperbol.: caelum, Auct. B. Hisp. 42 fin.—
Transf.: agmina vasto impetu,to drive asunder, scatter,: omnia Bacchanalia,i. e. to abolish,.—And in milit. lang.: aere dirutus, qs. ruined in pay, i. e. deprived of pay; said of a soldier whose pay was stopped as a punishment, Varr. ap. ; cf. Zumpt; cf. also beyond the milit. sphere, and without aere, of a bankrupt: homo diruptus dirutusque,both ruptured and bankrupt,.

la:noun:directio.html:
dīrectĭo, ōnis, f.
dirigo
(a very rare word).
A making straight or even, a levelling: plana coagmentorum,—
Concr., a straight line, App. de Mundo, p. 57.—
Trop.
A directing, aiming, towards any thing: quaedam rationis ad veritatem,.—
Righteousness, uprightness, ; .

la:verb:diripiendus.gloss: which is to be torn apart
senses: which is to be torn apart
which is to be laid waste
moving straight forward, in straight line
la:adv:directe.html:
dīrectē,
adv., directly, straight, etc., v. dirigo, P. a. fin. a.

la:noun:direptio.html:
dīreptĭo, ōnis, f.
diripio
,
a plundering, pillaging (rare, but good prose): urbs relicta direptioni et incendiis,; cf. urbis,; * : oppidi (with expugnatio),: profanorum sacrorumque,: sociorum (with vexatio),.—In plur., ; —
The stealing, rape: aurei velleris,.

la:noun:diritas.html:
dīrĭtas, ātis, f.
dirus
(rare but class.), lit. fearfulness, viz.,
Of fate, fatal mischief, misfortune: si qua invecta diritas casu foret, Cic. Poët. Tusc. 3, 14: totius diei,; cf. ominis,.—
Of character, fierceness, cruelty: omni diritate atque immanitate teterrimus,: quanta in altero diritas, in altero comitas!: morum (Tiberii),.

la:noun:direptor.html:
dīreptor, ōris, m.
id.
,
a plunderer (very rare; cf.: fur, praedo, raptor),; ; .
